Good morning. Our project is about learning from data where one class has far fewer examples than the other. We call the smaller class the minority class. Our method, CASB, adds examples for this class. I will explain how it works, compare it with other methods, and show both its strengths and limitations.

Imagine we have 100 examples. Ninety-five belong to one class and only five belong to the other. If a model always predicts the bigger class, it gets 95 answers right. But it misses every example from the smaller class. This is why high accuracy alone can be misleading. We want to find more minority cases without making too many wrong predictions. These numbers are an example, not an experiment result.

We have two main aims. First, we want to reduce confusion where the two classes are close together. Second, we want to support minority regions that have very few examples. This second problem is called intra-class imbalance: even inside the smaller class, some areas have many points and others have few. We also compare our versions across different models and scores. These are our aims; we do not claim to solve these problems completely.

ROS copies existing minority examples. SMOTE makes new points between two nearby minority points. Borderline-SMOTE focuses on minority points near mixed-class areas. ADASYN adds more points around cases that look difficult. Each choice has a weakness. For example, a difficult point might be useful, but it might also have a wrong label. Our method studies how to share the new points across different minority regions.

Earlier studies already looked at safe, boundary and sparse minority regions. Other methods changed where new points could be placed, or used model uncertainty to guide sampling. CASB builds on these ideas. Our focus is the particular way we combine source groups, generation rules and cleaning. We have not directly compared against every close earlier method, so that is still future work.

We collected 44 binary classification tasks. Binary means there are two classes. We used four classifiers. Four tasks had incomplete ADASYN results, so the main comparison uses the same 40 complete tasks for every method. Each task uses five supplied train-test splits and two random seeds. For Abalone, we changed the Sex category into numeric columns using only the training data. We kept failed runs visible instead of replacing them with guessed scores.

We first keep the test data aside. Inside the training data, we use a smaller validation part to choose how much oversampling to do. Then we train again using the chosen setting and measure the result on the untouched test data. Cleaning, scaling and oversampling learn only from training data. The two seeds reuse the same splits, so we must not treat every run as a new independent dataset.

We use four different classifiers. SVM learns a boundary between classes. KNN predicts from nearby examples. Random forest combines many decision trees. Logistic regression learns a simpler linear decision rule. Testing different classifiers helps us see whether a result depends on the model. We use the same outer train-test splits for a fair comparison.

Recall asks: of all real minority cases, how many did we find? Precision asks: of the cases we called minority, how many were correct? F1 combines precision and recall into one score. G-mean checks how well we detect both classes. Higher is better for each score here. We show all four because improving recall can sometimes reduce precision.

This picture shows the complete process. Start with training data, prepare the features, and measure the neighbourhood around minority points. Next, form three source groups and decide how many new points each group should produce. Choose a CASB version, make the new training set, and train the classifier. The test data is used only at the end to measure performance.

CASB means Coverage-Aware Safe-Border SMOTE. It makes two main choices. First: which minority point should we start from? Second: how far should we move toward another minority point? We use three groups to answer the first question. For some groups, the distance to the majority class limits the second choice. The word safe describes our intention. It does not mean every new point is guaranteed to have the right label.

For each minority point, we look at nearby training points. Coverage contains every minority point. Border contains points with a mixture of nearby majority and minority examples. Rare contains points whose minority neighbours are relatively far away. Border and rare also need enough nearby minority support. The groups can overlap: the same point may be in more than one group. Rare here means locally sparse, not a proven separate rare cluster.

The rings show which original points can be selected from each group. They are not new points. Coverage includes all minority points. Border focuses on mixed areas. Rare focuses on sparse areas. The same source can belong to several groups. Notice that being eligible does not guarantee a point will actually be selected.

Here is a small example. We have 100 majority points and 20 minority points. We want 75 minority points, so we need 55 new ones. Original CASB gives 28 additions to coverage, 16 to border and 11 to rare. These come from the 50, 30 and 20 percent weights, with rounding. We randomly choose sources within each group, and a source can be chosen again. If border or rare is empty, we choose from coverage but keep the original branch rule.

After choosing a source, we choose a nearby minority point. Usually we choose among up to five neighbours; the rare branch uses up to two. Let d be the distance to the closest majority point. A normal limited step can move at most half of d. A rare step can move at most 0.35 times d. Coverage points with very few majority neighbours can use the full line. For example, if d is two, the normal limited move is at most one unit. This limits movement but does not prove the new label is correct.

The new point lies on a straight line from the source to its chosen neighbour. Lambda tells us how far along that line to move. Zero means stay at the source, and one means reach the neighbour. SMOTE can use the whole line. Original CASB shortens the allowed part for some branches. Relaxed allows the whole line again. CASB-ROS stays at the source and makes a copy.

The three extra versions make small changes to the main idea. Relaxed changes the weights to 70, 20 and 10 percent and removes the movement limits. Edited first runs relaxed, then removes majority points that disagree with the local three-neighbour vote. It does not remove minority points. ROS uses the original 50, 30 and 20 weights but copies chosen sources instead of creating new locations.

This table puts the four versions side by side. C, B and R mean coverage, border and rare. The percentages tell us how to divide new additions, not how many original points belong to each group. Original CASB and CASB-ROS use the same weights. Relaxed and edited use different weights. Because relaxed changes both the weights and movement limits, we cannot say which change alone caused a result.

First look at the original data, then compare the other panels. SMOTE and the CASB interpolation versions add new locations. CASB-ROS adds copies at existing locations. Edited also removes some majority points. This is a constructed example to explain the process. It is not a real benchmark dataset and does not by itself show which method predicts best.

For a new point, we can check which source and neighbour were used, which group selected the source, and how far the point moved. This makes the generation process easier to inspect. The red-marked error was deliberately placed in this example. CASB did not discover that error. The figure shows that we can trace the process; it does not show that we can reliably detect noise.

Each coloured cell shows the average score of a CASB version minus a baseline score. A positive value means the CASB version scored higher. A negative value means it scored lower. This helps us see the tradeoffs. Do not look only at the positive cells: losses matter too. These are average differences, not statistical test results.

For each classifier and score, we pick the family version with the highest average and compare it with the strongest main baseline. Positive values favour our family. For random forest, F1 is slightly below the best baseline, even though the other three scores are higher. We chose the best version after seeing the results, so this table does not describe a method that chooses its version automatically before testing.

This experiment uses generated two-dimensional data so we can control how much the classes overlap. Smaller distance between the class centres means more overlap. Each curve shows one fixed method, and the panels show different classifiers. We use 20 seeds. The bands show uncertainty around the mean. This experiment studies overlap, not wrong training labels, and it is separate from the real-dataset benchmark.

Here we show the real Haberman dataset. Every panel uses the same PCA view, fitted on original training data. The resampling settings were chosen using training validation. We selected this example after seeing the results, so it is an illustration rather than independent evidence. Similar-looking clouds are expected because several methods use straight-line interpolation. The picture cannot prove that the labels of new points are correct.

For each dataset and score, we ask whether at least one CASB version beats all four main baselines. We count that as one family win. For random forest, the family wins on G-mean in 28 of the 40 datasets. The best version may differ from one dataset or score to another. Joint means the same version wins on both G-mean and F1. These are descriptive win counts, not counts of statistically proven wins.

Take one dataset and one score. Find the best CASB version, then find the strongest baseline. If the CASB score is strictly higher, count one family win. This checks what the family achieved after we saw the test results. It does not tell us how to choose the right version on new data. For that, we would need to select the version using training data only.

We first average the runs within each dataset. Friedman checks whether the methods differ somewhere across datasets. Wilcoxon compares a fixed CASB version with one baseline on paired datasets. Holm makes the significance rule stricter because we run many comparisons. We also check what happens when related datasets are grouped together. A significant test does not mean every CASB version is better.

This table counts the fixed-version comparisons that were significantly higher, significantly lower, or not significant after correction. All 16 Friedman tests found some difference between methods, but that does not identify CASB as the winner. A not-significant result means the test did not find strong enough evidence; it does not prove equality. When related tasks were grouped by their original source, no Wilcoxon comparison remained significant after correction, while the grouped sign test had nine significant results. So the conclusion depends on the test and how datasets are grouped.

There are four main limitations. First, a new point may still have the wrong label. Second, coverage can select noisy minority points, and edited does not remove them. Third, a straight line may be a poor path when a minority region is curved or split into separate areas. Fourth, some datasets are related, and the gains depend on the classifier and score. Next we should test stronger checks, better source selection, different generation paths, and new independent datasets.

CASB gives us a clear way to decide where new minority samples come from. The different versions show useful tradeoffs, especially between recall and precision. Random forest has 28 family G-mean wins out of 40 matched tasks. But we do not claim that CASB wins everywhere. Testing on new independent dataset sources is still important.

Thank you. I am happy to take questions about how we select sources, how the four versions differ, and how we measure the results. If asked whether CASB always beats SMOTE, the answer is no. Its benefit depends on the dataset, classifier and score. Our contribution is the implemented method and the measured tradeoffs.
